title: How Sītā is abducted
subject: narr:abduction-of-sita
question: What exactly does Rāvaṇa take, and does he touch Sītā?

rows.statement: Rāvaṇa approaches in the guise of a mendicant, reveals himself and seizes Sītā bodily — the description has him grasp her by the hair and the thighs — and carries her off through the sky in his chariot.

rows.locator: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam 3.8.74 (verse 3490), Caṭāyu uyir nītta paṭalam
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa does not touch Sītā: “the wicked one did not touch the jewelled lady, mindful of Brahmā’s word” (ayaṉ mēl urai, i.e. a curse), and with his pillar-like arms “dug up the ground a yojana below and above” and carried her off with it — the editor’s heading says, together with the leaf hut.

rows.locator: Araṇyakāṇḍa (commonly cited as sarga 7; not checked in an edition)
rows.statement: Before the golden-deer episode Rāma, knowing Rāvaṇa’s intention, tells Sītā to leave her shadow (chāyā) in the hut and to live hidden in the fire for a year; the illusory Sītā (māyā-Sītā) is the one Rāvaṇa carries off. Unlike the Kūrma Purāṇa, where Agni is the saviour, here Rāma himself devises the plan.

rows.locator: RCM Araṇyakāṇḍa, caupāīs before dohā 24 (common numbering)
rows.statement: While Lakṣmaṇa is away, Rāma tells Sītā to dwell in the fire until he has destroyed the rākṣasas; she enters the fire, leaving her own reflection (nija pratibimba), “of the same character, form and modesty.” Not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. Rāvaṇa abducts the reflection.
Rāvaṇa, a vidyādhara king, carries Sītā off to Laṅkā but does not force her; Jain tellings attribute his restraint to a vow taken before a Jain monk not to take a woman against her will.

note: Ramanujan (1991) and the essays in Richman (1991) use divergences like these to argue for many “tellings” rather than one original with deviations. The rows are not ranked; they show how each telling protects (or does not protect) Sītā’s inviolability by different means.

title: Who are Sītā’s parents?
subject: char:sita
question: How is Sītā born, and whose daughter (or sister) is she?

rows.statement: Janaka of Mithilā finds her in a furrow while ploughing the sacrificial ground; she is not born of a womb (ayonijā) and he raises her as his daughter.

She is the daughter of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī and his chief queen, sister of Rāma-paṇḍita and Lakkhaṇa; on their return from the Himalaya she is made queen consort. In the closing identification she is the mother of Rāhula in the Buddha’s last life.
She is the daughter of Janaka and Videhā, born as a twin with Bhāmaṇḍala, who is carried off at birth and raised among the vidyādharas.
She is born to Rāvaṇa’s queen Mandodarī; because she is foretold to cause Rāvaṇa’s ruin she is abandoned in a casket and found in Janaka’s realm, where she is raised.

rows.locator: sarga 8 (as summarised from Grierson’s and later accounts)
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa’s boon includes the condition that he will perish if he approaches his own daughter; his misdeeds lead to Sītā’s birth from his wife Mandodarī, and the sarga ends with Janaka finding her in a field being prepared for a sacrifice.
Nang Sida is born as Thotsakan’s daughter; because of an ill omen she is set adrift and is found and raised by King Chanok (Janaka). She is an incarnation of Laksami.
Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta, an incarnation of Nang Souxada — Indra’s wife, defiled by Hapmanasouane (Rāvaṇa), who vowed to take revenge in her next life as Sida.
Siti Dewi is presented in the summaries consulted as the adoptive daughter of Maharisi Kali; the details of her birth in the Laud-based text were not checked.

note: Two clusters stand out: tellings in which Sītā is found in the earth (Vālmīki and many Hindu tellings) and tellings in which she is Rāvaṇa’s own daughter (Guṇabhadra’s Jain line, the Adbhuta, Thai and Lao tellings), with the Buddhist jātaka making her Rāma’s sister. The table does not decide which is earlier.

title: Hanumān’s character
subject: char:hanuman
question: Who is Hanumān — what kind of being, what kind of devotee, and does he marry?

rows.locator: VR (CE) 4.65.8–28 (Jāmbavān’s account of his birth); Kiṣkindhā- and Sundarakāṇḍas
rows.statement: A vānara: Jāmbavān tells how the Wind god (Māruta) embraced Añjanā, wife of the monkey Kesarin, so that Hanumān is “Kesarin’s son by the field, Māruta’s own son” (kṣetraja / aurasa) and his equal in leaping; minister of Sugrīva, eloquent and learned, he leaps the ocean to find Sītā. No wife is mentioned.

rows.locator: RCM Sundarakāṇḍa passim; Uttarakāṇḍa before dohā 120(ka) for “rāma te adhika rāma kara dāsā”
rows.statement: The paradigmatic servant-devotee (dāsa) of Rāma. The Mānas also states in Kākabhuśuṇḍi’s discourse that “Rāma’s servant is greater than Rāma” — a general claim about devotees that later Hanumān devotion applied to him.

A vidyādhara prince — son of Pavanañjaya and Añjanā — not an animal; the monkey is his clan’s banner emblem. He marries (several wives in the Jain tradition) and at the end renounces the world as a Jain monk.

A brilliant white monkey warrior with a frankly amorous nature: he falls in love with the mermaid Suvannamaccha (Thotsakan’s daughter), fathering Macchanu, and in one episode takes Thotsakan’s form to sleep with his queen.

The Hanuman–Sovann Maccha romance during the building of the causeway, in which the mermaid princess steals the stones, falls in love with Hanuman and bears his son Macchanu, is one of the most loved episodes of Khmer performance; the standard written Reamker instead has Rāma compel the ocean god to cooperate.

note: Lutgendorf (2007) traces how a vānara minister became, in North India, a celibate god and the archetypal devotee, while Jain and Southeast Asian tellings made him a married or amorous hero. None of these is treated here as the “real” Hanumān.

title: Rāvaṇa’s portrayal
subject: char:ravana
question: What kind of being is Rāvaṇa, how is he judged, and who kills him?

rows.statement: A ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas, mighty through ascetic boons, learned yet given to lust and arrogance; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.

rows.locator: Rāvaṇa episodes and final battle (uddesas not checked)
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa is a vidyādhara king of the rākṣasa lineage and the eighth Prativāsudeva of Jain universal history; he is killed by Lakṣmaṇa (the Vāsudeva), not by Rāma, goes to hell for his violence, and will become a Tīrthaṅkara in the next ascending half-cycle. (Jain tradition also explains “ten-faced” by the reflection of his face in a necklace of nine gems — not checked here.)

A figure of tragic grandeur who, mindful of Brahmā’s word, does not touch Sītā (3.8.74); Rāma kills him with Brahmā’s weapon (6.36.191–196), and his queen Maṇṭōtari, lamenting that she had known Rāma to be Nārāyaṇa, dies embracing his body (6.36.243–244). Readers have long seen Kampaṉ’s Rāvaṇa as a tragic hero rather than a mere villain.

Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas of Laṅkā, ascends his Puṣpaka chariot, approaches the Buddha, circumambulates him, plays the vīṇā and sings verses (“I am Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked lord of the rākṣasas, come here”), and invites him to Laṅkā to teach; no abduction is narrated.
Thotsakan, the ten-faced king of Laṅkā, is Sida’s father; he keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanuman crushes it as Phra Ram’s arrows strike.

Hapmanasouane (Thôtsakane) is Phra Lam’s cousin; as Phra Lam is linked with a previous life of the Buddha, Hapmanasouane is compared with the Buddha’s cousin Devadatta (Phra Thevathat) or with Māra (Phra Man) — learned and powerful, but ruined by greed and desire.

title: Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā
subject: char:radha
question: Is Rādhā named, and what is her relation to Kṛṣṇa?

rows.statement: No gopī is named Rādhā. When Kṛṣṇa vanishes with one favoured gopī, the others say “surely the Lord Hari was worshipped (ārādhitaḥ) by her” (anayārādhito nūnam); later commentators read the verb as a veiled reference to Rādhā.

rows.locator: one verse (often cited as 1.89, Weber — unverified)
rows.statement: A single Prakrit verse speaks of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā (Rāhiā) as lovers — the earliest known literary mention, in an anthology whose date is disputed (before 640 CE).

The cowherd women dance the kuravai that Māyavaṉ danced with his elder brother and with Piññai (piññaiyōṭu āṭiya kuravai) in the cowherds’ settlement — a Tamil beloved of Kṛṣṇa who is not named Rādhā.
Āṇṭāḷ’s girls wake Nappiṉṉai, “daughter-in-law of Nandagopa”, on whose breast Kṛṣṇa lies, and call her “Nappiṉṉai, lady, Tiru (Śrī)!” to intercede for them; Rādhā does not appear.
Rādhā is the heroine: the poem follows her longing, jealousy, the messages of her friend and her reunion with Kṛṣṇa, who is her lover, not her husband.

rows.locator: Brahma-khaṇḍa, Prakṛti-khaṇḍa and Kṛṣṇajanma-khaṇḍa (chapters not checked)
rows.statement: Rādhā is the main goddess, inseparable from Kṛṣṇa and dwelling with him in Goloka, the personification of mūlaprakṛti; in the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa she heads the five forms of Prakṛti (Rādhā, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī), and “every insult to a woman is an offence against Rādhā”. (Popular summaries add that Brahmā performs her marriage to Kṛṣṇa — not checked here.)

Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti (power of bliss); Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one in identity, separated eternally and are reunited in Caitanya, who is Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā’s sentiment and complexion, come to taste her love.
Śaṅkaradeva’s Ekaśaraṇa devotion centres on Kṛṣṇa alone; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside him in this tradition.

note: The table shows Rādhā absent (Bhāgavata), marginal (Gāhā Sattasaī), central as beloved (Gītagovinda), supreme goddess (Brahmavaivarta) and theological principle (Caitanya Caritāmṛta), alongside Tamil tellings with a different beloved (Piññai / Nappiṉṉai) and an Assamese tradition that deliberately leaves her out.

title: Who kills Rāvaṇa?
subject: narr:lanka-war
question: Who defeats the king of Laṅkā (or his double), and how?

rows.statement: Reminded by Mātali to use Brahmā’s weapon, Rāma fires the Brahmā-made arrow first given him by Agastya; it pierces Rāvaṇa’s heart and he falls from his chariot “like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt”.
Rāma kills Rāvaṇa; the poem makes the battle a display of Rāma’s divine līlā.
Rāma fits Brahmā’s weapon to his bow and releases it; it enters Rāvaṇa’s breast and drinks his life. Maṇṭōtari then dies embracing the body (6.36.244).
Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa, as in all Jain universal history the Vāsudeva kills the Prativāsudeva; Rāma, a non-violent Baladeva, later becomes a monk and attains liberation.

After the ten-headed Rāvaṇa is dead, his elder brother, the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa of Puṣkara, scatters Rāma’s army and strikes Rāma unconscious; Sītā takes the form of Mahākālī and severs his thousand heads.
Śāraḷā Dāsa narrates a further war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of Vilaṅkā; who strikes the final blow was not checked.
Phra Ram’s arrows cannot kill Thotsakan until Hanuman obtains and crushes the heart that Thotsakan has kept outside his body.
There is no Rāvaṇa and no war: the story ends with the return from exile and Rāma-paṇḍita’s long reign.

title: Murukaṉ and Skanda across texts
subject: deity:murugan
question: How is the Tamil god Murukaṉ presented, and when does he carry Skanda’s attributes?

rows.statement: Cēyōṉ, “the red one,” presides over the hill (kuṟiñci) landscape, one of four deities assigned to landscapes; no mythology is given. The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses him as “red Murukaṉ.”

Eight of the surviving poems are to Cevvēḷ (Murukaṉ) — beside six to Tirumāl and others to the river Vaiyai — praising him at Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam (“cool Paraṅkuṉṟu”, likened to the Himalaya) near Madurai; poem 5 narrates his birth from Śiva’s seed, the northern myth.

rows.locator: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, c. ll. 91–102 (the six faces) and the description of the twelve hands
rows.statement: A guide-poem leading the devotee to Murukaṉ’s shrines: each of his six faces has its own function (one radiates light, one grants boons, one guards the brāhmaṇs’ sacrifices …), he has twelve hands, and he is the “lord of six (faces) borne by six (mothers)” — Skanda’s Kṛttikā iconography in a Tamil poem.

The hill women dance the kuravai praising the vēl of the god who never leaves Centil, Ceṅkōṭu, Veṇkuṉṟu and Ērakam, the white-bladed spear that once slew Cūr in the sea; he has six faces and twelve hands and was nursed by six mothers in the Saravaṇa pool; the Vēlaṉ priest is called for the possession-dance (veṟiyāṭal).
A full Tamil Skanda Purāṇa: birth from Śiva’s fiery seed, the war against Cūrapatmaṉ, and marriages to Teyvāṉai (Indra’s daughter) and the Tamil hunter girl Vaḷḷi.

Skanda is born of Agni’s seed, gathered by Svāhā in the forms of the ṛṣis’ wives (a star passage adds birth from Rudra in the Gaṅgā and among the Kṛttikās); the spilled (skanna) seed gives his name, the Mothers attend him, Indra consecrates him general (senāpati) of the gods, and the Kṛttikās go to heaven — there is no Tamil Vaḷḷi.

note: Read in sequence these rows support the scholarly account of convergence (Zvelebil 1973; Clothey 1978): a Tamil hill god acquires Skanda’s myth and iconography by the late Caṅkam period. The identification is recorded as IDENTIFIED_WITH, not as a merger.
